deep.reconstruction:
Context: bundle R.Minimal, Riemann's notes for the posthumous memoir on minimal surfaces ('Über die Fläche vom kleinsten Inhalt bei gegebener Begrenzung', ed. Hattendorff 1867). The previous page introduces auxiliary surface parameters p, q and the notation (∂f ∂g) = (f_p g_q − f_q g_p) dp dq. It also wants area integrals of such Jacobians turned into boundary integrals, without case-by-case discussion of orientation. This page supplies the general lemma and begins its justification.

(1) General principle. If the integrand of a multiple integral is a functional (Jacobian) determinant, and one wants to integrate with respect to one of the functions, one must first write the determinant as a sum of derivatives (a divergence). This is 'Jacobi's rule'.

(2) Two-dimensional case. Riemann's identity is
f_p g_q − f_q g_p = ∂(f g_q)/∂p − ∂(f g_p)/∂q.
[Mine:] Expanding the right side gives f_p g_q + f g_qp − f_q g_p − f g_pq. The mixed terms cancel by equality of mixed partials.
Hence ∬(∂f ∂g) = ∬[∂_p(f g_q) − ∂_q(f g_p)] dp dq. Here 'integration with respect to f' means removing f from under the derivative, so f appears undifferentiated in a boundary term.

(3) Choice of coordinates. One may choose the curve families (p), (q) so that p is constant on the boundary.

(4) n-dimensional case (right column). Let R = Σ± ∂f_1/∂x_1 ⋯ ∂f_n/∂x_n = det(∂f_i/∂x_j). Riemann claims
R = ∂/∂x_1 ( f_1 Σ± ∂f_2/∂x_2 ⋯ ∂f_n/∂x_n ) + ∂/∂x_2 ( f_1 ∂R/∂(∂f_1/∂x_2) ) + ∂/∂x_3 ( f_1 ∂R/∂(∂f_1/∂x_3) ) + ⋯
That is, R = Σ_j ∂_j (f_1 C_{1j}), where C_{1j} = ∂R/∂(∂f_1/∂x_j) is the cofactor; the first term is the case j = 1.
He states that this follows from the theorem Σ_{i=1..n} ∂/∂x_i ( ∂R/∂(∂f_1/∂x_i) ) = 0.
[Mine:] By Laplace expansion along the first row, R = Σ_j (∂f_1/∂x_j) C_{1j}. The C_{1j} contain only f_2, …, f_n. The product rule then gives Σ_j ∂_j(f_1 C_{1j}) = R + f_1 Σ_j ∂_j C_{1j} = R.

(5) Existence of the coordinate system, argued for a simply connected surface. Shrink the surface by moving the whole boundary inward simultaneously until it collapses to a point. During this:
- the surface is not cut into pieces; for a multiply connected surface its connectivity is not changed;
- the distances between simultaneous positions of corresponding boundary elements stay everywhere in finite ratios to one another.
The process can continue until the surface becomes a point (simply connected case) or a system of lines (multiply connected case). Labelling the successive boundary curves by a monotone parameter p:
- p is constant on the original boundary;
- p has a single interior maximum or minimum (simply connected case);
- the strip between (p) and (p+dp) is nowhere infinitely thin compared with its width elsewhere.

Purpose, carried out on the next page: q is taken along the trajectories of boundary points, and p increases from inside to outside. Integrating ∂_p(f g_q) over p gives the boundary term ∮ f g_q dq. [Mine:] The contribution at the centre vanishes because the curve (p) degenerates to a point there. The ∂_q term integrates to 0 over the closed curves p = const. This yields ∬(∂f ∂g) = ∮ f dg, with orientation fixed by the convention on ∂p, ∂q.
errors: First line of the right column: the last factor of R appears to be written ∂f_n/∂x_2 (with a struck-out symbol); it should be ∂f_n/∂x_n. This is a slip of the pen.
In the 'Satz', f should be f_1, i.e. Σ_i ∂_i(∂R/∂(∂f_1/∂x_i)) = 0. This is notational only.

The existence of the shrinking deformation is asserted as 'offenbar' without proof. No condition is given that makes the level curves smooth, single-valued and free of critical points other than one extremum. For multiply connected surfaces the limiting 'line system' gives a degenerate set where p is not regular. This is heuristic, not a proof.

Implicit and unstated: the q-coordinate is singular at the extremum point (polar-like), and q is not single-valued (the next page notes its jump). The vanishing of the inner boundary term f g_q at the collapsed point is not addressed on this page.

results.what: Jacobian determinant written as a divergence: det(∂f_i/∂x_j) = Σ_j ∂_j(f_1·cofactor_{1j}); in 2D, f_p g_q − f_q g_p = ∂_p(f g_q) − ∂_q(f g_p)
results.modern_name: Jacobian as exact form / divergence form of the Jacobian (d(f_1 df_2∧…∧df_n) = df_1∧…∧df_n)

results.what: Σ_i ∂_i(∂R/∂(∂f_1/∂x_i)) = 0 (divergence-free rows of the cofactor matrix)
results.modern_name: Piola identity / Jacobi's identity for cofactors (d∘d = 0)

results.what: Area integral of a Jacobian equals a boundary integral, ∬(∂f ∂g) = ∮ f dg, proved via special coordinates (p constant on boundary)
results.modern_name: Green's / Stokes' theorem for 2-forms (∫_S df∧dg = ∮ f dg)
results.usually_credited_to: Green 1828, Stokes/Kelvin 1850s; Riemann used Green-type lemmas in his 1851 dissertation

results.what: Construction of a curve system by shrinking the boundary uniformly to a point (or line system), giving a parameter p constant on the boundary with a single interior extremum
results.modern_name: Collar/level-set foliation; an exhaustion function with a single critical point (Morse-type) used to prove Stokes' theorem
results.usually_credited_to: No specific attribution; such foliation arguments are informal precursors of later differential-topological constructions

deep.surprise_reason: The Jacobian-as-divergence identity is Jacobi's (1841) and Green/Stokes-type boundary conversion is standard and known in Riemann's work. The only mildly unusual element is the heuristic proof via a boundary-shrinking foliation with one interior extremum and a remark on multiply connected surfaces. That is a nice unpublished detail, not a major result.

r,t=symbols('r t',positive=True); f=r**2*cos(t); g=r*sin(t); x=r*cos(t); y=r*sin(t); jac=Matrix([[diff(x,r),diff(x,t)],[diff(y,r),diff(y,t)]]).det(); lhs=integrate(integrate((diff(f,r)*diff(g,t)-diff(f,t)*diff(g,r)),(r,0,1)),(t,0,2*pi)); rhs=integrate((f*diff(g,t)).subs(r,1),(t,0,2*pi)); simplify(lhs-rhs)
checkable.asserts: Example of ∬(∂f ∂g) = ∮ f dg in coordinates p=r (constant on boundary, extremum at centre), q=t; result 0
